vignette: He is twelve when the shouting first fractures the house. The walls are thin, the floorboards groan under heavy pacing. He learns to read the rhythm of violence before he masters long division. Glass shatters against plaster. Boots stamp against hardwood. He spends those years becoming a ghost in his own home, moving through rooms like a draft, keeping his eyes on the scuffed linoleum, counting ceiling cracks until the noise stops. When his mother finally leaves, taking his younger sister with her in the dead of a November night, he doesn't cry. He just folds his hands and waits for the next storm. Decades pass, but the body never forgets. Elias works his way through high school and into the military, where the rigid structure feels like armor. He learns to march, to listen for orders, to keep his chest stiff. After service, he marries, divorces, and takes jobs that demand he show up whether he feels ready or not. The years stack up like unopened crates, but the old wiring remains. He is seventy-nine, African, divorced, and still measures his life in shifts. Now, at the distribution center on the edge of the city, he still shows up. He drives a forklift, checks inventory logs, and supervises a crew of younger men. The warehouse is vast, all corrugated steel and humming refrigeration units, but to him, it feels too small. Fluorescent lights buzz like trapped insects. The sound of pallets dropping echoes like furniture being dragged across a floor. He walks the aisles with his head slightly turned, eyes scanning the overhead racks, shoulders hunched as if ready to shield someone from a falling beam. He doesn't talk much about the past. When he does, his voice stays level, but his fingers trace the same seam on his work pants, over and over. He hasn't slept through the night in thirty years. Sometimes, the old house returns in fragments: the smell of stale whiskey, the flick of a match, the sudden stillness before a strike. He wakes drenched, heart hammering against his ribs, and sits on the edge of his bed until his breathing evens out. His ex-wife's neighborhood, where he once left everything behind, now feels like a territory he must actively avoid. He routes his afternoon drives three blocks out of his way. At work, he declines team lunches. He stands by the loading bay doors, watching the street, listening for footsteps that match the heavy tread from his youth. When a supervisor claps him on the shoulder to ask about a shipment, Elias flinches, then forces a nod, muttering something about inventory. He doesn't dislike the younger workers. He just can't bear the sudden movements, the raised voices, the unpredictable shifts in tone. They are too loud, too close to what he has spent a lifetime outrunning. In the clinic, he sits across from me with his spine straight, hands folded, gaze fixed on the middle distance. He tells me about the morning air biting through his jacket, about the coffee he drinks black to keep his hands steady. He doesn't need me to fix the quiet. He just needs it to be the right kind. When the session ends, he stands, adjusts his cap, and walks to the door with his usual measured steps. He doesn't look back.
